question: The recent EU regulation governing the welfare and traceability of dogs and cats introduces important tools to improve animal identification procedures and crack down on the illegal pet trade.

However, the cross-border trafficking of dogs of all ages and other pets remains a profitable source of income for criminal organisations, which take advantage of fake papers, online platforms and the fact that checks are not always up to scratch. This trade is, among other things, fuelling the exploitation of animals by beggars. In the light of the above: 1.

What measures will the Commission take to ensure that the Regulation in question is applied uniformly and that national databases are interoperable, thereby enabling the competent authorities to promptly establish the validity of foreign animal passports and ascertain their holders’ country of origin?

Will it step up cooperation between Europol and veterinary, customs, police and local authorities to combat the illegal trafficking of pets, prevent beggars from taking advantage of these animals and crack down on online pet sales?
Will the Commission monitor the effectiveness of the new regulatory framework and propose additional initiatives to bolster efforts to tackle the unlawful practices mentioned above?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) 1. The primary responsibility for implementing and enforcing EU legislation in the area of animal welfare lies with the Member States.

The Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, ensures consistent application across the EU through monitoring and by verifying the functioning of national control systems, and making publicly available the reports of audits in Member States1,2.

Regulation (EU) 2026/18183 requires all Member States, by August 2030, to establish national databases for registering dog and cat microchips, and the Commission, by August 2031, to establish an index database ensuring the interoperability of those national databases4.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1818 also requires that the Commission, by August 2036, establishes a EU pet traveller database5, which will facilitate detection of commercial imports disguised as travels with a pet. 2. Illegal movement of pets is addressed by Europol under the EMPACT Environmental Crime priority6.

To strengthen cross-border cooperation, the Commission also established the EU Pet Animals Network (PAN)7, to support administrative assistance, rapid information sharing and coordinated enforcement on breaches of EU rules on dog and cat health and welfare.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1818 sets specific rules for the verification of the authenticity of the identification, registration and ownership of dogs and cats advertised online. 3. By 31 August 2040, Regulation (EU) 2026/1818 requires the Commission to carry out an evaluation of the Regulation, including an assessment of the reduction of illegal trade in dogs and cats8.
1 Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2017 on official

controls and other official activities performed to ensure the application of food and feed law, rules on animal health and welfare, plant health and plant protection products, OJ L 95, 7.4.2017, p. 1, https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0625-20250105. 2 Audit Reports - Food Audits and Analysis https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/index.cfm.

3 Regulation (EU) 2026/1818 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2026 on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability; OJ L, 2026/1818, 10.8.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1818/oj. 4 Articles 23(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2026/1818. 5 Article 26(4) of Regulation (EU) 2026/1818. 6 https://www.europol.europa.eu/how-we-work/empact. 7 https://food.ec.europa.
